name: Tagabawa
catalog_citation: DuBois, Carl D. & Lauretta J. DuBois. 2006. Phonemic Statement of Tagabawa. 1st ed. Manila: Summer Institute of Linguistics Philippines. 19 pp. ISBN 978-971-18-0406-0. SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 35849 (data 1987-88, Malasila, Makilala, Cotabato).
catalog_locator: §2 'Stress', p. 10 of 19 (PDF p. 10; page image rendered and read during this reading; scanned copy)
catalog_quote: The analysis of stress is based on a corpus of more than 2,600 Tagabawa words. An additional 600 words were excluded from analysis as being borrowed from Spanish, English or Cebuano Visayan. Stress consists of an increase in intensity and a raising of pitch. Stress also consists of vowel length in open (CV) syllables. Of the Tagabawa corpus of polysyllabic words, stress occurs as follows: on penultimate syllables: 92% (approximately 2400 words) on ultimate syllables: 8% (approximately 200 words) on antepenultimate syllables: less than 1/2 of 1% (8 words) Although stress is predominantly penultimate, it is phonemic, as evidenced by the following minimally and nearly minimally contrastive pairs of words. [ˈʔaːtod˺] /ˈʔatod/ ‘look at’ [ʔaˈtod˺] /ʔaˈtod/ ‘stump’ [ˈkaːpi] /ˈkapi/ ‘hawk’ [kaˈpiː] /kaˈpi/ ‘coffee’ [taˈgaːnaʔ˺] /taˈganaʔ/ ‘prepare’ [tagaˈnaʔ˺] /tagaˈnaʔ/ ‘orig.people’ [ˈpaːlad˺…

An additional 600 words were excluded.. borrowed from Spanish, English or Cebuano Visayan. Stress consists of an increase in intensity and a raising of pitch. Stress also consists of vowel length in open (CV) syllables. Of the Tagabawa corpus of polysyllabic words, stress occurs as follows: on penultimate sy…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is contrastive (phonemic) but heavily skewed: in a corpus of >2,600 native polysyllabic words it falls on the penult in 92%, on the final syllable in 8%, and on the antepenult in 8 words; a stressed open syllable is lengthened, but length is never independently contrastive. Eight (near-)minimal pairs penult vs. final are given.
new_statements.exceptions: 8% final-stressed words and 8 antepenult-stressed words (all native); about 600 loans from Spanish, English and Cebuano were excluded from the count. Grammar Essentials (1991, p. 4) and Tagabawa Texts (2005, p. 2) add only that stress is phonemic and left unwritten in the orthography.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation/lexical forms (wordlist corpus); vowel length tied to open stressed syllables. Sentence intonation is described separately in Grammar Essentials §6.1 (high pitch on the stressed syllable of the last word). The 1892 Gisbert dictionary prologue notes accent on the syllable preceding a geminate consonant (penult), consistent with the modern default.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding source describes Tagabawa as spoken in Sitio Lambac, Malasila, Makilala, (North) Cotabato, and states it is assumed to hold for the whole language (Kidapawan to Toril, south of Mt Apo); only /l/~/r/ regional variation is noted. Same languoid as Glottolog taga1272 (ISO bgs). It is distinct from Guiangan/Klata 'Bagobo' (gian1240), which the authors explicitly separate; Gisbert 1892's 'Bagobo' (Sibulan/Tibbison/Tuban, Davao) is tagged Tagabawa by Project Gutenberg/DuBois.

sources.note: Section 2 'Stress' (p. 10): stress = intensity + pitch raise (+ vowel length in open syllables); corpus of >2,600 words: 92% penultimate, 8% ultimate, <0.5% antepenultimate (8 words); 'predominantly penultimate' but phonemic, with 8 (near-)minimal pairs (ˈʔatod 'look at' vs ʔaˈtod 'stump', ˈkapi 'hawk' vs kaˈpi 'coffee', etc.); length only in open stressed syllables, never contrastive on its own.

sources.note: Introduction/orthography (pdf p. 4): 'Although stress is phonemic, it has not been marked as such in the language examples cited throughout this description.' Section 6.1 (pdf p. 24): in statements high pitch falls on the stressed syllable of the last word of the sentence, low pitch on the final (post-stress) syllable; questions raise pitch on the penultimate syllable of the final word.

sources.note: Prologue 'Al lector': in words with a hyphen between identical consonants (od-do, gon-nao) the consonant sounds in both syllables, 'si bien en ésta [la sílaba anterior] es en donde especialmente se carga el acento' — accent on the syllable before the geminate (penult); no general rule. Variety: Bagobo of Sibulan, Tibbison, Tuban (Davao).
